requirements.product_understanding: A global video platform that enables creators to upload on-demand videos (VOD) or stream live content, while allowing viewers to watch seamlessly on any device regardless of network conditions. The platform automatically adjusts video quality based on the viewer's bandwidth to ensure optimal viewing experience.
users_and_use_cases: Creators upload VOD content and manage their video library
Creators go live and broadcast real-time video streams
Viewers watch VOD videos on demand
Viewers watch live streams in real-time
Platform operations monitor system performance and manage content delivery
Viewers switch between different quality levels based on network conditions
functional: Support VOD upload and playback functionality for creators and viewers
Enable live streaming capabilities with real-time broadcast
Implement adaptive bitrate streaming that automatically adjusts video quality based on available bandwidth
Provide cross-device compatibility for viewing on various platforms
Ensure live stream latency remains under 10 seconds glass-to-glass
Support global audience access with worldwide content delivery
non_functional: Maintain 99.95% availability for live streaming services
Handle peak traffic of 5,000 concurrent live streams
Ensure adaptive bitrate functionality works seamlessly across different network conditions
assumptions: The platform will use existing CDN infrastructure or similar content delivery mechanisms
Video encoding and transcoding capabilities are available through existing services or can be implemented
The platform will support standard video formats and protocols for compatibility
Network bandwidth measurements and quality detection methods are available or can be implemented
Global content distribution requirements can be met with current infrastructure capabilities

components.name: Upload Manager
components.description: Handles video upload and initial processing for both VOD and live streams. Processes incoming media files, extracts metadata, and validates content before triggering transcoding pipelines. For live streams, it manages the initial connection and stream validation. This component is the single point of entry for all content to the platform and must scale horizontally to handle peak live streaming loads of 5,000 concurrent streams while maintaining low latency for VOD uploads. It's designed as a stateless service with horizontal scaling capability, using a message queue for load distribution and ensuring that no single point of failure exists in the upload process. The service is not responsible for content delivery or transcoding - it only initiates those processes. It must be able to handle 500MB/s of concurrent uploads during peak live streaming periods with an availability target of 99.95% for live streams and 99.9% for VOD uploads. The component uses a queue-based approach for managing the limited resource of available transcoding slots, ensuring that no two streams can be processed simultaneously in the same transcoding queue. This is critical because it prevents overloading the transcoding infrastructure during peak load periods while maintaining quality and consistency across all content ingestion processes.

components.name: Transcoding Service
components.description: Responsible for converting uploaded videos into multiple bitrates and formats for adaptive streaming. Processes both VOD content and live stream segments, generating HLS or DASH manifests with multiple quality levels. This service is designed as a stateless, horizontally scalable microservice that can handle high-throughput video processing workloads. It uses a distributed task queue to manage transcoding jobs and ensures that each job is processed exactly once. The service must support real-time processing of live streams while maintaining the 10-second glass-to-glass latency target for live broadcasts. It implements a simple queuing mechanism with basic priority scheduling for transcoding jobs, ensuring no race conditions occur during processing operations. The component is designed to scale independently from other services and can handle up to 5,000 concurrent transcoding jobs during peak live streaming periods while maintaining consistent quality output for both VOD and live content. It's built with a focus on resource efficiency to stay within the $200,000 monthly budget constraint by optimizing compute usage through dynamic scaling based on job queue depth.

components.name: Content Delivery Network
components.description: Distributes video content globally using edge nodes for optimal performance and low latency. Manages caching strategies, manifest delivery, and bandwidth adaptation for viewers. This component is the core of the adaptive bitrate functionality and must support seamless quality switching based on real-time network conditions. It's designed as a distributed system with multiple geographic regions to ensure global coverage and low-latency access for all users. The CDN handles both VOD and live stream delivery, implementing smart caching policies that adapt to viewer behavior patterns and content popularity trends. It uses a single-writer per manifest approach for managing manifest updates to prevent race conditions during live streaming where multiple segments are being updated simultaneously. This ensures consistency in quality switching and prevents viewers from experiencing playback issues due to manifest corruption or inconsistent segment availability. The system is designed to maintain 99.9% availability for VOD content and 99.95% for live streams while operating within the specified budget constraints by implementing intelligent resource allocation based on geographic demand patterns.

components.name: Live Stream Manager
components.description: Manages real-time streaming sessions, including connection handling, stream validation, and quality adaptation for live broadcasts. This is the core component that ensures the 10-second glass-to-glass latency target for live streams. It maintains persistent connections with broadcasters using a connection pooling strategy to handle up to 5,000 concurrent streams efficiently without resource contention. The service implements a gRPC streaming channel for real-time communication between broadcasters and the platform, enabling immediate quality adjustments based on bandwidth measurements. It uses a message queue-based approach for stream status updates instead of maintaining persistent WebSocket connections for each stream, allowing horizontal scaling through connection managers rather than increasing connection count per node. The component must handle up to 5,000 concurrent live streams with minimal latency while maintaining high availability requirements of 99.95% for live services. It's designed as a stateful service that tracks session metadata and stream health metrics to ensure optimal delivery quality.

components.name: Viewer Experience Service
components.description: Provides the interface layer for viewers to access video content, including playback controls, quality selection, and bandwidth detection. This component handles all viewer-facing interactions and implements the adaptive bitrate algorithm that switches between quality levels based on real-time network conditions. It's designed as a stateless service that can scale horizontally to support 2 million concurrent VOD viewers while maintaining responsive performance for live stream viewers. The service uses a WebSocket-based persistent connection to enable real-time quality adjustments and provides a REST API for standard playback operations. It implements a hybrid approach combining client-side measurements with server-side throughput testing and adaptive algorithms to improve accuracy of bandwidth detection. The component is responsible for measuring bandwidth and network conditions using both client-side techniques and CDN performance metrics, and implementing intelligent quality switching algorithms that balance performance with user experience. It's designed to maintain 99.9% availability for VOD services and 99.95% for live streams while operating within the specified budget constraints by optimizing resource usage through efficient caching and load distribution.

components.name: Resource Manager
components.description: Centralized service that manages transcoding slot allocation and other limited resources across all ingestion and processing components. This service acts as a single point of truth for resource access, eliminating duplication between Upload Manager and previous Transcoding Scheduler. It uses a simple queuing mechanism with basic priority scheduling to ensure consistent, conflict-free access to transcoding resources while maintaining the required availability targets. The component is designed to be highly available with multi-AZ replication and automatic failover to prevent single points of failure in resource management. It implements rate limiting per creator to prevent abuse and ensures that no two streams can be processed simultaneously in the same transcoding queue, which is critical for maintaining quality during peak live streaming loads of 5,000 concurrent streams.

architecture.infrastructure: The platform uses a hybrid cloud infrastructure with compute nodes distributed across multiple geographic regions. The core services are containerized using Kubernetes for horizontal scaling and resource management. CDN infrastructure is leveraged for global content delivery with edge nodes optimized for low-latency streaming. Storage is implemented using object storage with automatic tiering between hot and cold storage based on access patterns. The system uses a message queue-based architecture for inter-service communication, ensuring loose coupling and fault tolerance. All components are designed with auto-scaling capabilities to handle traffic spikes while maintaining cost efficiency within the $200,000 monthly budget constraint. The infrastructure is built using a microservices pattern that allows independent scaling of different components based on their specific load requirements and availability targets.

decisions.decision: Use atomic claims for managing limited resources in transcoding slots
decisions.alternatives_considered: Optimistic locking with retry, single-writer per shard, distributed locks using Redis
decisions.trade_offs: Atomic claims provide the strongest consistency guarantees but require more complex implementation than optimistic locking. Single-writer per shard is simpler but may not scale as well under high contention.
decisions.rationale: The platform must ensure no two streams can be processed simultaneously in the same transcoding queue, which is critical for maintaining quality and preventing resource exhaustion during peak live streaming loads of 5,000 concurrent streams. Atomic claims provide the necessary guarantee that no race conditions occur when accessing these limited resources.

decisions.decision: Implement gRPC streaming for live stream communication channels
decisions.alternatives_considered: WebSocket with JSON messages, REST polling, UDP-based protocols
decisions.trade_offs: gRPC streaming requires more complex client-side implementation than WebSocket but provides better performance and reliability for real-time updates. REST polling would introduce unnecessary latency.
decisions.rationale: The 10-second glass-to-glass latency target for live streams requires a persistent communication channel that can handle real-time updates with minimal delay. gRPC streaming provides the necessary low-latency, high-throughput communication while maintaining the reliability needed for broadcast-quality streaming services.

decisions.decision: Use optimistic lock with retry mechanism for concurrent resource access
decisions.alternatives_considered: Pessimistic locking, distributed locks, atomic operations
decisions.trade_offs: Optimistic locking introduces retries but provides better performance under normal conditions. Pessimistic locking can cause deadlocks and reduce throughput.
decisions.rationale: The platform handles high-concurrency scenarios during peak live streaming periods where multiple processes may attempt to access shared resources simultaneously. Optimistic locking with retry provides the best balance of performance and consistency while maintaining the required availability targets for both VOD (99.9%) and live (99.95%) services.

decisions.decision: Implement single-writer per manifest for manifest updates during live streaming
decisions.alternatives_considered: Multi-writer with conflict resolution, distributed consensus protocols, optimistic concurrency control
decisions.trade_offs: Single-writer per manifest is simpler to implement but requires careful shard management. Distributed consensus protocols provide stronger guarantees but add complexity and latency.
decisions.rationale: Live stream manifest updates must be consistent and predictable to ensure viewers don't experience playback issues due to corrupted or inconsistent segment information. The single-writer per manifest approach provides the necessary consistency guarantee while maintaining performance requirements for real-time updates during live broadcasts.

decisions.decision: Use queue-based approach for streaming endpoint management
decisions.alternatives_considered: Distributed atomic claims, simple counters with locks, connection pooling
decisions.trade_offs: Queue-based approach provides better scalability than distributed atomic claims but requires more complex implementation. Connection pooling is simpler but may not provide the necessary isolation.
decisions.rationale: Streaming endpoints are more abundant than transcoding slots, so the overhead of distributed atomic claims is not justified and creates unnecessary complexity. A queue-based approach allows for efficient assignment of streaming endpoints while maintaining simplicity and scalability.

decisions.alternatives_considered: Separate Upload Manager and Transcoding Scheduler, single monolithic service
decisions.trade_offs: Decomposition increases system complexity but improves fault isolation and reduces coupling. Monolithic approach is simpler but creates tight coupling between upload processing and transcoding resource management.
decisions.rationale: The previous separation created duplication in transcoding slot management responsibilities. Consolidating into a single Resource Manager service eliminates the duplicated responsibility while maintaining clear separation of concerns for other functions. This improves reliability by reducing potential points of failure and ensures consistent resource allocation.

security_controls.threat_model_summary: Primary threats include unauthorized content access (creators' private content leaked, live streams intercepted), DoS attacks on ingestion/transcoding services during peak live streams, credential theft from broadcaster authentication, and CDN-based content tampering. Live stream integrity is critical due to 10-second latency requirement - any disruption could cause broadcast failures. VOD content may be targeted for piracy distribution through manifest manipulation or unauthorized access.
security_controls.authentication: OAuth2 with short-lived JWTs (30-minute expiry) validated at API Gateway, with Upload Manager handling broadcaster authentication via HMAC-signed tokens using shared secrets stored in HashiCorp Vault. Viewer authentication uses anonymous access with device fingerprinting for abuse detection, while creator authentication uses OAuth2 with refresh tokens and session management at Viewer Experience Service. HMAC tokens now include 10-minute TTL with unique nonces to prevent replay attacks and token blacklist cache (Redis) that allows immediate invalidation of tokens during live streams.
security_controls.authorization: Role-based access control (RBAC) implemented at API Gateway level with creator roles having full access to their own content, platform ops having administrative privileges, and viewers having read-only access to public content. Ingestion Service enforces content ownership checks using JWT claims, Transcoding Service validates stream ownership via HMAC tokens and implements explicit content ownership validation by querying the Upload Manager or a shared metadata store using the video_id from the HMAC token, Live Stream Manager uses queue-based approach for endpoint assignment with role-based validation, Viewer Experience Service implements manifest-level authorization based on content access policies. Each service explicitly validates JWT claims to prevent privilege escalation.
security_controls.iam: Centralized IAM using Auth0 for OAuth2 provider with custom claims in JWTs. Creator accounts are managed through Auth0 user pools with MFA required for admin operations. Platform ops use service accounts with least-privilege access and temporary credentials via AWS STS. All secrets (API keys, HMAC secrets) stored in HashiCorp Vault with automated rotation every 90 days. Encryption keys are now managed using AWS KMS with key aliases that support seamless key rotation without service interruption and version tracking for all encrypted data.
security_controls.network_boundaries: API Gateway acts as perimeter firewall with rate limiting and WAF rules for all external traffic. Internal services communicate over mTLS using Istio service mesh with mutual authentication and encrypted communication between pods. Upload Manager and Transcoding Service are in separate VPC subnets with security groups restricting access to only necessary internal services. Live Stream Manager uses dedicated subnet with strict ingress/egress rules for WebSocket connections. Strict firewall rules are enforced at VPC level for each service.
security_controls.secrets_and_encryption: All secrets managed through HashiCorp Vault with automated rotation, including HMAC secrets, database credentials, and CDN tokens. Data at rest encrypted using AWS S3 server-side encryption with KMS keys, data in transit encrypted using TLS 1.3 for all external communications and mTLS between services. Database connections use SSL/TLS with certificate validation, and all internal service-to-service communication uses mutual TLS authentication. Encryption keys are now managed separately from Vault using AWS KMS with multi-key rotation strategy.

reliability_design.scaling_strategy: The platform implements horizontal scaling across all components with auto-scaling groups based on CPU, memory, and queue depth metrics. The Upload Manager scales to handle 500MB/s peak upload throughput with dedicated Kubernetes pods that can scale from 10 to 200 instances during live peaks. Transcoding Service uses dynamic scaling based on job queue depth, ranging from 50 to 500 instances to process up to 5,000 concurrent transcoding jobs. Content Delivery Network leverages existing CDN infrastructure with edge nodes that automatically scale based on geographic demand. Live Stream Manager scales with Kubernetes deployments, using stateful sets for session tracking with 20-100 pods during peak live streams. Viewer Experience Service scales horizontally to handle 2M concurrent VOD viewers with up to 500 pods in auto-scaling groups. All services use message queues (RabbitMQ) for load distribution and loose coupling, ensuring no single component becomes a bottleneck.
reliability_design.reliability: The platform achieves 99.9% availability for VOD and 99.95% for live through redundant deployments across 3 availability zones in each region with auto-recovery mechanisms. Upload Manager implements circuit breaker patterns and retry logic with exponential backoff to handle transient failures. Transcoding Service uses distributed task queues with idempotent processing to prevent duplicate work and ensure job completion even during partial failures. Live Stream Manager maintains persistent connections with WebSocket fallbacks and gRPC streaming channels with automatic failover to backup endpoints within 2 seconds to meet the 10-second glass-to-glass target. Content Delivery Network leverages multi-region CDN infrastructure with automatic failover to secondary regions when primary nodes fail. Viewer Experience Service implements optimistic locking with retry mechanisms for concurrent updates, ensuring no race conditions during quality adjustments. All components use simple queuing mechanisms for managing limited resources (transcoding slots, streaming endpoints) to prevent resource exhaustion and maintain consistent service quality.
reliability_design.disaster_recovery: For VOD services, the platform implements continuous replication with real-time or near-real-time backup mechanisms for VOD assets to achieve an RPO of less than 15 minutes. For live streams, the platform uses a multi-region failover strategy where each live stream session is replicated to secondary regions within 5 seconds of primary region failure. The Upload Manager maintains a backup queue in Redis for processing jobs during primary service outages, with automatic failover to secondary clusters within 30 seconds. Transcoding Service uses a distributed task queue with job persistence that survives cluster failures, ensuring no transcoding work is lost during regional outages. Live Stream Manager implements cross-region replication of stream sessions with automatic failover to backup endpoints within 2 seconds of primary region failure. Viewer Experience Service maintains session state in Redis clusters with multi-region replication for seamless user experience during outages. All components use automated monitoring and alerting systems that trigger failover procedures within 5 minutes of detecting service degradation.
reliability_design.observability: The platform implements comprehensive observability using Prometheus for metrics collection, Grafana for dashboard visualization, and ELK stack for log aggregation. Key metrics include: Upload Manager - upload throughput (MB/s), queue depth, error rates; Transcoding Service - job processing time, queue depth, success/failure rates; Live Stream Manager - connection stability, latency (glass-to-glass), session count; Content Delivery Network - cache hit ratio, latency, bandwidth utilization; Viewer Experience Service - quality switching frequency, buffering events, user session duration. All services implement distributed tracing using OpenTelemetry with automatic correlation of requests across components. Health checks are implemented at every service level with automated alerts for availability thresholds below 99.9% for VOD and 99.95% for live streams. Real-time monitoring dashboards track system performance and user experience metrics, with automated incident response procedures triggered when availability targets are breached. A hierarchical alerting system with severity levels is implemented to prevent alert fatigue during incidents. Specific observability for adaptive bitrate performance including quality switching frequency, buffering events, and user-reported quality issues is now included.
failure_scenarios: Upload Manager fails during peak live streaming: The service uses simple queuing mechanisms to manage transcoding slots, preventing resource contention. When a node fails, the distributed task queue automatically reassigns pending jobs to healthy nodes within 30 seconds, maintaining 99.95% availability for live streams.

Transcoding Service experiences partial outage: The system uses idempotent processing with job persistence in distributed queues, ensuring no work is lost during failures. Auto-scaling groups maintain service capacity at 100% during outages, and backup transcoding clusters handle overflow within 2 minutes to meet availability targets.

Live Stream Manager connection drops during broadcast: The system uses gRPC streaming channels with automatic failover to backup endpoints within 2 seconds (reduced from 5 seconds). Session state is maintained in Redis clusters with multi-region replication, ensuring seamless continuation of live streams with minimal disruption to viewers.

CDN edge node failure affects global delivery: The platform leverages multi-region CDN infrastructure with automatic failover to secondary regions within 10 seconds. Cache invalidation and manifest updates use single-writer per manifest approach to prevent corruption during failover, maintaining 99.9% availability for VOD and 99.95% for live streams.

Viewer Experience Service experiences high latency: The system uses optimistic locking with retry mechanisms and implements circuit breaker patterns to prevent cascading failures. When latency exceeds 100ms, the service automatically switches to degraded mode with pre-cached quality levels, maintaining 99.9% availability for VOD and 99.95% for live streams.

Database connection failure in Viewer Preference service: The system uses Redis clusters with multi-region replication and automatic failover within 30 seconds. Session data is replicated across multiple regions to ensure no loss of user preferences during database failures, maintaining consistent quality switching behavior.

findings.issue: HMAC-signed tokens for broadcaster authentication lack proper nonce validation and are vulnerable to replay attacks despite the addition of nonces.
findings.recommendation: Implement a more robust replay protection mechanism using a distributed nonce store (e.g., Redis with TTL) that tracks used nonces per stream key, ensuring each nonce is consumed only once within its TTL window. This prevents replay attacks while maintaining the low-latency requirements of live streaming.

findings.issue: The Transcoding Service validates stream ownership via HMAC tokens but does not enforce a strict separation between creator and platform ops roles, potentially allowing unauthorized access to transcoding resources.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit role validation in the Transcoding Service to ensure that only creators or platform ops with appropriate permissions can initiate transcoding jobs for specific videos. This includes validating JWT claims against a centralized RBAC policy at the point of job initiation.

findings.issue: The API Gateway is described as acting as a perimeter firewall, but there's no mention of how it handles internal service-to-service communication security or micro-segmentation.
findings.recommendation: Implement network segmentation using Kubernetes Network Policies or similar mechanisms to restrict inter-service communication at the pod level. Ensure that all internal communications between services are encrypted and authenticated, even within the same VPC.

findings.issue: While AWS KMS is used for encryption keys, there's no indication of key rotation policies or how keys are rotated in practice, which could lead to long-term exposure if not properly managed.
findings.recommendation: Establish an automated key rotation policy using AWS KMS key rotation features with a defined schedule (e.g., every 90 days) and implement monitoring alerts for upcoming key expiration or failed rotations. Ensure that all services are configured to automatically fetch new keys during rotation events.

findings.issue: The Viewer Experience Service uses anonymous access with device fingerprinting for abuse detection, but there's no mention of how user sessions or preferences are protected from unauthorized modification.
findings.recommendation: Implement session-based authentication for viewer preference updates and ensure that all changes to viewer preferences are validated against the authenticated user's identity. Additionally, consider adding rate limiting and anomaly detection on preference update endpoints to prevent abuse.

findings.issue: The transcoding service is the most expensive component, estimated at $120,000-$140,000/month. With 5,000 concurrent live streams and 2M VOD viewers, this service must handle massive compute loads. The budget allocation for transcoding is tight but feasible with efficient resource utilization.
findings.recommendation: Implement advanced dynamic scaling and consider using spot instances or reserved capacity to optimize costs while maintaining required performance.

findings.issue: CDN costs are estimated at $40,000-$50,000/month. With global audience access and adaptive bitrate streaming, bandwidth usage will be substantial. The budget allows for CDN costs but leaves little headroom for traffic spikes.
findings.recommendation: Implement aggressive caching strategies and content tiering to reduce CDN egress costs.

findings.issue: The live stream manager requires 5,000 concurrent connections with 10-second glass-to-glass latency target. This component is critical for maintaining service availability at 99.95% and requires dedicated infrastructure to handle high connection counts.
findings.recommendation: Ensure sufficient WebSocket connection handling capacity and implement connection pooling to manage resource usage efficiently.

findings.issue: The resource manager component is critical for managing transcoding slots and ensuring no race conditions occur. While not the most expensive component, it's essential for system reliability and must be highly available with multi-AZ replication.
findings.recommendation: Monitor resource contention closely to prevent bottlenecks during peak loads.

findings.issue: The Resource Manager component is described as a centralized service managing transcoding slot allocation and other limited resources. While it's designed to be highly available with multi-AZ replication, the consolidation of ingestion service components into this single service creates a potential SPOF for resource management during peak live streaming loads.
findings.recommendation: Implement a distributed resource management approach using a consensus-based system (like Raft or Paxos) or a distributed lock manager instead of a single centralized Resource Manager. This would eliminate the single point of failure while maintaining the required consistency guarantees for transcoding slot allocation. Alternatively, if keeping the centralized approach, implement a true multi-master setup with automatic failover and cross-region replication to ensure no single point of failure exists.

findings.issue: The platform claims 99.95% availability for live streams but has a 2-second failover time for Live Stream Manager that may not be sufficient to maintain the 10-second glass-to-glass latency target under all failure scenarios, particularly during regional outages or CDN edge node failures.
findings.recommendation: Review and optimize the live stream failover mechanism to ensure it consistently meets the 10-second glass-to-glass requirement. Consider implementing a more aggressive pre-failover strategy where backup endpoints are proactively prepared, or reduce the failover time to less than 1 second to provide headroom for network propagation delays.

findings.issue: While disaster recovery is described with RPO < 15 minutes for VOD and multi-region failover for live streams, there's no explicit mention of backup strategies for the actual video content itself beyond replication. The system relies heavily on CDN infrastructure for delivery but doesn't specify how content integrity is maintained during regional failures.
findings.recommendation: Implement a tiered backup strategy including regular snapshots of video assets with automated validation checks, and establish clear procedures for restoring content from backup in case of complete regional outages. Additionally, define specific recovery time objectives (RTO) for different types of content assets to ensure alignment with the overall availability targets.

findings.issue: The architecture describes several failure scenarios but lacks a comprehensive failure mode analysis that includes potential cascading failures between components, particularly around the message queue system which is used by multiple services for load distribution.
findings.recommendation: Conduct a formal failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA) to identify potential cascading failures involving the RabbitMQ-based message queues. Implement circuit breaker patterns at service boundaries that consume messages from these queues, and establish monitoring thresholds that trigger immediate alerting when queue depths exceed predefined limits.

findings.issue: While comprehensive observability is described, there's no specific mention of how the system handles the adaptive bitrate switching behavior under stress conditions or how it detects degradation in quality switching performance that could impact user experience.
findings.recommendation: Add specific metrics and alerts for adaptive bitrate performance including quality switching frequency, buffering events, and user-reported quality issues. Implement synthetic monitoring of actual playback scenarios to detect when adaptive bitrate algorithms are not performing as expected under varying network conditions.

findings.issue: The architecture incorrectly assumes REST POST-per-event is acceptable for live streaming with 10-second glass-to-glass latency requirement. The proposed API uses REST endpoints for upload progress tracking and stream status updates, which introduces unnecessary round-trips and violates the real-time communication requirements.
findings.recommendation: Replace REST polling with gRPC streaming or WebSocket connections for all real-time communication. Specifically, change /videos/{id}/upload to use a persistent WebSocket connection (like existing /streams/{id}/live) and implement proper gRPC streaming for status updates instead of REST POST endpoints that send one event at a time.

findings.issue: The architecture duplicates transcoding slot management responsibilities between Upload Manager and Resource Manager, despite the decision to consolidate ingestion services. Both components are designed to manage transcoding resources, creating a structural coupling that violates the principle of single responsibility.
findings.recommendation: Remove Upload Manager's transcoding resource management logic entirely. All transcoding slot allocation should be handled by Resource Manager alone, with Upload Manager only handling initial validation and job queuing. This eliminates race conditions between services and simplifies the architecture.

findings.issue: The Content Delivery Network is described as a single distributed system with 'multiple geographic regions' but lacks explicit load balancing or sharding mechanisms for handling 2 million concurrent VOD viewers. The architecture assumes existing CDN infrastructure will handle all traffic without specifying how it scales to meet peak demand.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit CDN load balancing and edge node distribution strategies that scale with traffic patterns. Implement dynamic content routing based on geographic proximity and viewer behavior, with auto-scaling of edge nodes proportional to concurrent viewership peaks.

findings.issue: The architecture defines 99.9% availability for VOD but 99.95% for live streams while both are critical services. However, the reliability design assumes identical failure recovery mechanisms for both services, which is inconsistent with their different SLA requirements.
findings.recommendation: Implement separate reliability strategies for VOD and live services. Live services should have additional redundancy (e.g., 3x replication instead of 2x) and faster failover mechanisms to meet the stricter 99.95% availability target, while VOD can use more cost-effective redundancy patterns.

findings.issue: The architecture uses atomic claims for transcoding slot management with complex distributed locking mechanisms that create unnecessary complexity and potential performance bottlenecks. The system is designed to handle 5,000 concurrent streams but the resource allocation mechanism is overly complex for this scale.
findings.recommendation: Simplify transcoding resource management using a basic queuing approach with priority scheduling instead of atomic claims. Implement a simple slot-based queue that allows multiple streams to be queued and processed sequentially without complex distributed locking, reducing complexity and improving performance.

findings.issue: The architecture assumes bandwidth detection methods are 'available or can be implemented' but doesn't specify how the system will handle variable network conditions across global users with different ISPs, mobile networks, and device capabilities. This creates a potential point of failure for adaptive bitrate functionality.
findings.recommendation: Implement multiple bandwidth measurement techniques including client-side throughput testing, CDN performance metrics, and server-side validation to provide robust quality switching. Add fallback mechanisms when primary measurement methods fail.

findings.issue: The Live Stream Manager is described as stateful but uses a queue-based approach for endpoint management instead of maintaining persistent session data. This creates inconsistency between the service's stateful nature and its implementation approach.
findings.recommendation: Clarify whether Live Stream Manager maintains session state in Redis or other persistent storage, and ensure this aligns with the queue-based endpoint assignment strategy. Either make the service truly stateless by moving session data to external storage, or implement proper state management with consistent session tracking.

architecture_stages.characteristics: A minimal viable platform with core VOD functionality and basic live streaming support. Focus on validating the concept with essential features while reducing complexity and cost.
architecture_stages.purpose: Validate product-market fit with minimal investment, focusing on core user flows and essential infrastructure.
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: After 3 months of operation with 100 active creators and 50,000 VOD views/month, demonstrating stable performance under initial load conditions while staying within $200,000 monthly budget constraints.

architecture_stages.characteristics: Enhanced platform supporting full VOD and live streaming capabilities with improved scalability, additional features, and better resource management. Maintains core architecture but adds capacity for increased traffic.
architecture_stages.purpose: Scale to support growing user base and traffic demands while maintaining performance and reliability standards.
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When concurrent live streams exceed 2,000 and VOD viewership reaches 1 million concurrent users, indicating need for expanded infrastructure and improved resource allocation strategies.

architecture_stages.characteristics: Highly distributed platform with regional partitioning, specialized services, and advanced content delivery strategies to handle global scale requirements. Includes microservices for specific functions like bandwidth detection, manifest management, and quality optimization.
architecture_stages.purpose: Support global audience with peak loads of 5,000 concurrent live streams and 2 million VOD viewers while maintaining SLA targets across multiple geographic regions.
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When system shows sustained performance degradation under peak load conditions (latency > 15 seconds for live streams, bandwidth adaptation failures exceeding 2% of sessions) or when operational costs exceed $200,000/month due to inefficient resource utilization.

blueprint.product: A global video platform that enables creators to upload on-demand videos (VOD) or stream live content, while allowing viewers to watch seamlessly on any device regardless of network conditions. components.name: Upload Manager
components.description: Handles video upload and initial processing for both VOD and live streams. Processes incoming media files, extracts metadata, and validates content before triggering transcoding pipelines. For live streams, it manages the initial connection and stream validation. This component is the single point of entry for all content to the platform and must scale horizontally to handle peak live streaming loads of 5,000 concurrent streams while maintaining low latency for VOD uploads. It's designed as a stateless service with horizontal scaling capability, using a message queue for load distribution and ensuring that no single point of failure exists in the upload process. The service is not responsible for content delivery or transcoding - it only initiates those processes. It must be able to handle 500MB/s of concurrent uploads during peak live streaming periods with an availability target of 99.95% for live streams and 99.9% for VOD uploads. The component uses a queue-based approach for managing the limited resource of available transcoding slots, ensuring that no two streams can be processed simultaneously in the same transcoding queue. This is critical because it prevents overloading the transcoding infrastructure during peak load periods while maintaining quality and consistency across all content ingestion processes.

components.name: Transcoding Service
components.description: Responsible for converting uploaded videos into multiple bitrates and formats for adaptive streaming. Processes both VOD content and live stream segments, generating HLS or DASH manifests with multiple quality levels. This service is designed as a stateless, horizontally scalable microservice that can handle high-throughput video processing workloads. It uses a distributed task queue to manage transcoding jobs and ensures that each job is processed exactly once. The service must support real-time processing of live streams while maintaining the 10-second glass-to-glass latency target for live broadcasts. It implements a simple queuing mechanism with basic priority scheduling for transcoding jobs, ensuring no race conditions occur during processing operations. The component is designed to scale independently from other services and can handle up to 5,000 concurrent transcoding jobs during peak live streaming periods while maintaining consistent quality output for both VOD and live content. It's built with a focus on resource efficiency to stay within the $200,000 monthly budget constraint by optimizing compute usage through dynamic scaling based on job queue depth.

components.name: Content Delivery Network
components.description: Distributes video content globally using edge nodes for optimal performance and low latency. Manages caching strategies, manifest delivery, and bandwidth adaptation for viewers. This component is the core of the adaptive bitrate functionality and must support seamless quality switching based on real-time network conditions. It's designed as a distributed system with multiple geographic regions to ensure global coverage and low-latency access for all users. The CDN handles both VOD and live stream delivery, implementing smart caching policies that adapt to viewer behavior patterns and content popularity trends. It uses a single-writer per manifest approach for managing manifest updates to prevent race conditions during live streaming where multiple segments are being updated simultaneously. This ensures consistency in quality switching and prevents viewers from experiencing playback issues due to manifest corruption or inconsistent segment availability. The system is designed to maintain 99.9% availability for VOD content and 99.95% for live streams while operating within the specified budget constraints by implementing intelligent resource allocation based on geographic demand patterns.

components.name: Live Stream Manager
components.description: Manages real-time streaming sessions, including connection handling, stream validation, and quality adaptation for live broadcasts. This is the core component that ensures the 10-second glass-to-glass latency target for live streams. It maintains persistent connections with broadcasters using a connection pooling strategy to handle up to 5,000 concurrent streams efficiently without resource contention. The service implements a gRPC streaming channel for real-time communication between broadcasters and the platform, enabling immediate quality adjustments based on bandwidth measurements. It uses a message queue-based approach for stream status updates instead of maintaining persistent WebSocket connections for each stream, allowing horizontal scaling through connection managers rather than increasing connection count per node. The component must handle up to 5,000 concurrent live streams with minimal latency while maintaining high availability requirements of 99.95% for live services. It's designed as a stateful service that tracks session metadata and stream health metrics to ensure optimal delivery quality.

components.name: Viewer Experience Service
components.description: Provides the interface layer for viewers to access video content, including playback controls, quality selection, and bandwidth detection. This component handles all viewer-facing interactions and implements the adaptive bitrate algorithm that switches between quality levels based on real-time network conditions. It's designed as a stateless service that can scale horizontally to support 2 million concurrent VOD viewers while maintaining responsive performance for live stream viewers. The service uses a WebSocket-based persistent connection to enable real-time quality adjustments and provides a REST API for standard playback operations. It implements a hybrid approach combining client-side measurements with server-side throughput testing and adaptive algorithms to improve accuracy of bandwidth detection. The component is responsible for measuring bandwidth and network conditions using both client-side techniques and CDN performance metrics, and implementing intelligent quality switching algorithms that balance performance with user experience. It's designed to maintain 99.9% availability for VOD services and 99.95% for live streams while operating within the specified budget constraints by optimizing resource usage through efficient caching and load distribution.

components.name: Resource Manager
components.description: Centralized service that manages transcoding slot allocation and other limited resources across all ingestion and processing components. This service acts as a single point of truth for resource access, eliminating duplication between Upload Manager and previous Transcoding Scheduler. It uses a simple queuing mechanism with basic priority scheduling to ensure consistent, conflict-free access to transcoding resources while maintaining the required availability targets. The component is designed to be highly available with multi-AZ replication and automatic failover to prevent single points of failure in resource management. It implements rate limiting per creator to prevent abuse and ensures that no two streams can be processed simultaneously in the same transcoding queue, which is critical for maintaining quality during peak live streaming loads of 5,000 concurrent streams.

security_controls.threat_model_summary: Primary threats include unauthorized content access (creators' private content leaked, live streams intercepted), DoS attacks on ingestion/transcoding services during peak live streams, credential theft from broadcaster authentication, and CDN-based content tampering. Live stream integrity is critical due to 10-second latency requirement - any disruption could cause broadcast failures. VOD content may be targeted for piracy distribution through manifest manipulation or unauthorized access.
security_controls.authentication: OAuth2 with short-lived JWTs (30-minute expiry) validated at API Gateway, with Upload Manager handling broadcaster authentication via HMAC-signed tokens using shared secrets stored in HashiCorp Vault. Viewer authentication uses anonymous access with device fingerprinting for abuse detection, while creator authentication uses OAuth2 with refresh tokens and session management at Viewer Experience Service. HMAC tokens now include 10-minute TTL with unique nonces to prevent replay attacks and token blacklist cache (Redis) that allows immediate invalidation of tokens during live streams.
security_controls.authorization: Role-based access control (RBAC) implemented at API Gateway level with creator roles having full access to their own content, platform ops having administrative privileges, and viewers having read-only access to public content. Ingestion Service enforces content ownership checks using JWT claims, Transcoding Service validates stream ownership via HMAC tokens and implements explicit content ownership validation by querying the Upload Manager or a shared metadata store using the video_id from the HMAC token, Live Stream Manager uses queue-based approach for endpoint assignment with role-based validation, Viewer Experience Service implements manifest-level authorization based on content access policies. Each service explicitly validates JWT claims to prevent privilege escalation.
security_controls.iam: Centralized IAM using Auth0 for OAuth2 provider with custom claims in JWTs. Creator accounts are managed through Auth0 user pools with MFA required for admin operations. Platform ops use service accounts with least-privilege access and temporary credentials via AWS STS. All secrets (API keys, HMAC secrets) stored in HashiCorp Vault with automated rotation every 90 days. Encryption keys are now managed using AWS KMS with key aliases that support seamless key rotation without service interruption and version tracking for all encrypted data.
security_controls.network_boundaries: API Gateway acts as perimeter firewall with rate limiting and WAF rules for all external traffic. Internal services communicate over mTLS using Istio service mesh with mutual authentication and encrypted communication between pods. Upload Manager and Transcoding Service are in separate VPC subnets with security groups restricting access to only necessary internal services. Live Stream Manager uses dedicated subnet with strict ingress/egress rules for WebSocket connections. Strict firewall rules are enforced at VPC level for each service.
security_controls.secrets_and_encryption: All secrets managed through HashiCorp Vault with automated rotation, including HMAC secrets, database credentials, and CDN tokens. Data at rest encrypted using AWS S3 server-side encryption with KMS keys, data in transit encrypted using TLS 1.3 for all external communications and mTLS between services. Database connections use SSL/TLS with certificate validation, and all internal service-to-service communication uses mutual TLS authentication. Encryption keys are now managed separately from Vault using AWS KMS with multi-key rotation strategy.

threats.issue: HMAC-signed tokens for broadcaster authentication lack proper nonce validation and are vulnerable to replay attacks despite the addition of nonces.
threats.recommendation: Implement a more robust replay protection mechanism using a distributed nonce store (e.g., Redis with TTL) that tracks used nonces per stream key, ensuring each nonce is consumed only once within its TTL window. This prevents replay attacks while maintaining the low-latency requirements of live streaming.

threats.issue: The Transcoding Service validates stream ownership via HMAC tokens but does not enforce a strict separation between creator and platform ops roles, potentially allowing unauthorized access to transcoding resources.
threats.recommendation: Add explicit role validation in the Transcoding Service to ensure that only creators or platform ops with appropriate permissions can initiate transcoding jobs for specific videos. This includes validating JWT claims against a centralized RBAC policy at the point of job initiation.

threats.issue: The API Gateway is described as acting as a perimeter firewall, but there's no mention of how it handles internal service-to-service communication security or micro-segmentation.
threats.recommendation: Implement network segmentation using Kubernetes Network Policies or similar mechanisms to restrict inter-service communication at the pod level. Ensure that all internal communications between services are encrypted and authenticated, even within the same VPC.

threats.issue: While AWS KMS is used for encryption keys, there's no indication of key rotation policies or how keys are rotated in practice, which could lead to long-term exposure if not properly managed.
threats.recommendation: Establish an automated key rotation policy using AWS KMS key rotation features with a defined schedule (e.g., every 90 days) and implement monitoring alerts for upcoming key expiration or failed rotations. Ensure that all services are configured to automatically fetch new keys during rotation events.

threats.issue: The Viewer Experience Service uses anonymous access with device fingerprinting for abuse detection, but there's no mention of how user sessions or preferences are protected from unauthorized modification.
threats.recommendation: Implement session-based authentication for viewer preference updates and ensure that all changes to viewer preferences are validated against the authenticated user's identity. Additionally, consider adding rate limiting and anomaly detection on preference update endpoints to prevent abuse.

blueprint.infrastructure: The platform uses a hybrid cloud infrastructure with compute nodes distributed across multiple geographic regions. The core services are containerized using Kubernetes for horizontal scaling and resource management. CDN infrastructure is leveraged for global content delivery with edge nodes optimized for low-latency streaming. Storage is implemented using object storage with automatic tiering between hot and cold storage based on access patterns. The system uses a message queue-based architecture for inter-service communication, ensuring loose coupling and fault tolerance. All components are designed with auto-scaling capabilities to handle traffic spikes while maintaining cost efficiency within the $200,000 monthly budget constraint. The infrastructure is built using a microservices pattern that allows independent scaling of different components based on their specific load requirements and availability targets.
blueprint.scaling_strategy: The platform implements horizontal scaling across all components with auto-scaling groups based on CPU, memory, and queue depth metrics. The Upload Manager scales to handle 500MB/s peak upload throughput with dedicated Kubernetes pods that can scale from 10 to 200 instances during live peaks. Transcoding Service uses dynamic scaling based on job queue depth, ranging from 50 to 500 instances to process up to 5,000 concurrent transcoding jobs. Content Delivery Network leverages existing CDN infrastructure with edge nodes that automatically scale based on geographic demand. Live Stream Manager scales with Kubernetes deployments, using stateful sets for session tracking with 20-100 pods during peak live streams. Viewer Experience Service scales horizontally to handle 2M concurrent VOD viewers with up to 500 pods in auto-scaling groups. All services use message queues (RabbitMQ) for load distribution and loose coupling, ensuring no single component becomes a bottleneck.
blueprint.reliability: The platform achieves 99.9% availability for VOD and 99.95% for live through redundant deployments across 3 availability zones in each region with auto-recovery mechanisms. Upload Manager implements circuit breaker patterns and retry logic with exponential backoff to handle transient failures. Transcoding Service uses distributed task queues with idempotent processing to prevent duplicate work and ensure job completion even during partial failures. Live Stream Manager maintains persistent connections with WebSocket fallbacks and gRPC streaming channels with automatic failover to backup endpoints within 2 seconds to meet the 10-second glass-to-glass target. Content Delivery Network leverages multi-region CDN infrastructure with automatic failover to secondary regions when primary nodes fail. Viewer Experience Service implements optimistic locking with retry mechanisms for concurrent updates, ensuring no race conditions during quality adjustments. All components use simple queuing mechanisms for managing limited resources (transcoding slots, streaming endpoints) to prevent resource exhaustion and maintain consistent service quality.
blueprint.disaster_recovery: For VOD services, the platform implements continuous replication with real-time or near-real-time backup mechanisms for VOD assets to achieve an RPO of less than 15 minutes. For live streams, the platform uses a multi-region failover strategy where each live stream session is replicated to secondary regions within 5 seconds of primary region failure. The Upload Manager maintains a backup queue in Redis for processing jobs during primary service outages, with automatic failover to secondary clusters within 30 seconds. Transcoding Service uses a distributed task queue with job persistence that survives cluster failures, ensuring no transcoding work is lost during regional outages. Live Stream Manager implements cross-region replication of stream sessions with automatic failover to backup endpoints within 2 seconds of primary region failure. Viewer Experience Service maintains session state in Redis clusters with multi-region replication for seamless user experience during outages. All components use automated monitoring and alerting systems that trigger failover procedures within 5 minutes of detecting service degradation.
blueprint.observability: The platform implements comprehensive observability using Prometheus for metrics collection, Grafana for dashboard visualization, and ELK stack for log aggregation. Key metrics include: Upload Manager - upload throughput (MB/s), queue depth, error rates; Transcoding Service - job processing time, queue depth, success/failure rates; Live Stream Manager - connection stability, latency (glass-to-glass), session count; Content Delivery Network - cache hit ratio, latency, bandwidth utilization; Viewer Experience Service - quality switching frequency, buffering events, user session duration. All services implement distributed tracing using OpenTelemetry with automatic correlation of requests across components. Health checks are implemented at every service level with automated alerts for availability thresholds below 99.9% for VOD and 99.95% for live streams. Real-time monitoring dashboards track system performance and user experience metrics, with automated incident response procedures triggered when availability targets are breached. A hierarchical alerting system with severity levels is implemented to prevent alert fatigue during incidents. Specific observability for adaptive bitrate performance including quality switching frequency, buffering events, and user-reported quality issues is now included.

When a node fails, the distributed task queue automatically reassigns pending jobs to healthy nodes within 30 seconds, maintaining 99.95% availability for live streams.

Transcoding Service experiences partial outage: The system uses idempotent processing with job persistence in distributed queues, ensuring no work is lost during failures. decisions.decision: Use atomic claims for managing limited resources in transcoding slots
decisions.alternatives_considered: Optimistic locking with retry, single-writer per shard, distributed locks using Redis
decisions.trade_offs: Atomic claims provide the strongest consistency guarantees but require more complex implementation than optimistic locking. Single-writer per shard is simpler but may not scale as well under high contention.
decisions.rationale: The platform must ensure no two streams can be processed simultaneously in the same transcoding queue, which is critical for maintaining quality and preventing resource exhaustion during peak live streaming loads of 5,000 concurrent streams. Atomic claims provide the necessary guarantee that no race conditions occur when accessing these limited resources.

decisions.decision: Implement gRPC streaming for live stream communication channels
decisions.alternatives_considered: WebSocket with JSON messages, REST polling, UDP-based protocols
decisions.trade_offs: gRPC streaming requires more complex client-side implementation than WebSocket but provides better performance and reliability for real-time updates. REST polling would introduce unnecessary latency.
decisions.rationale: The 10-second glass-to-glass latency target for live streams requires a persistent communication channel that can handle real-time updates with minimal delay. gRPC streaming provides the necessary low-latency, high-throughput communication while maintaining the reliability needed for broadcast-quality streaming services.

decisions.decision: Use optimistic lock with retry mechanism for concurrent resource access
decisions.alternatives_considered: Pessimistic locking, distributed locks, atomic operations
decisions.trade_offs: Optimistic locking introduces retries but provides better performance under normal conditions. Pessimistic locking can cause deadlocks and reduce throughput.
decisions.rationale: The platform handles high-concurrency scenarios during peak live streaming periods where multiple processes may attempt to access shared resources simultaneously. Optimistic locking with retry provides the best balance of performance and consistency while maintaining the required availability targets for both VOD (99.9%) and live (99.95%) services.

decisions.decision: Implement single-writer per manifest for manifest updates during live streaming
decisions.alternatives_considered: Multi-writer with conflict resolution, distributed consensus protocols, optimistic concurrency control
decisions.trade_offs: Single-writer per manifest is simpler to implement but requires careful shard management. Distributed consensus protocols provide stronger guarantees but add complexity and latency.
decisions.rationale: Live stream manifest updates must be consistent and predictable to ensure viewers don't experience playback issues due to corrupted or inconsistent segment information. The single-writer per manifest approach provides the necessary consistency guarantee while maintaining performance requirements for real-time updates during live broadcasts.

decisions.decision: Use queue-based approach for streaming endpoint management
decisions.alternatives_considered: Distributed atomic claims, simple counters with locks, connection pooling
decisions.trade_offs: Queue-based approach provides better scalability than distributed atomic claims but requires more complex implementation. Connection pooling is simpler but may not provide the necessary isolation.
decisions.rationale: Streaming endpoints are more abundant than transcoding slots, so the overhead of distributed atomic claims is not justified and creates unnecessary complexity. A queue-based approach allows for efficient assignment of streaming endpoints while maintaining simplicity and scalability.

decisions.alternatives_considered: Separate Upload Manager and Transcoding Scheduler, single monolithic service
decisions.trade_offs: Decomposition increases system complexity but improves fault isolation and reduces coupling. Monolithic approach is simpler but creates tight coupling between upload processing and transcoding resource management.
decisions.rationale: The previous separation created duplication in transcoding slot management responsibilities. Consolidating into a single Resource Manager service eliminates the duplicated responsibility while maintaining clear separation of concerns for other functions. This improves reliability by reducing potential points of failure and ensures consistent resource allocation.
